reference.source: Textbook of Pediatric Rheumatology / ILAR & PRINTO criteria
clinicalPearls: A monogenic autoinflammatory vasculopathy caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in the ADA2 gene (formerly CECR1)
Presents in childhood with a polyarteritis-nodosa-like small- and medium-vessel vasculitis, livedo racemosa and recurrent fevers
Early-onset ischaemic and haemorrhagic strokes, often affecting the deep brain (lacunar strokes), are a hallmark and can be recurrent

A wide phenotype also includes immunodeficiency with recurrent infections and low immunoglobulins, and haematological features such as cytopenias, bone marrow failure or features resembling pure red cell aplasia
Diagnosis rests on genetic testing for ADA2 variants together with demonstration of low serum ADA2 enzyme activity
TNF inhibition is highly effective at preventing strokes and controlling vasculitis and is preferred over corticosteroids for long-term control

Antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy is generally avoided because of the risk of haemorrhagic stroke, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is considered for severe haematological or immune disease
reference.pathophysiology: Deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 results from biallelic mutations in the ADA2 gene, reducing the activity of a secreted enzyme important for endothelial integrity and the differentiation of monocytes and macrophages. Loss of ADA2 skews monocytes towards a proinflammatory phenotype with excess tumour necrosis factor, causing endothelial damage and a systemic vasculopathy affecting small and medium vessels. This produces the polyarteritis-nodosa-like vasculitis, cutaneous livedo and, through injury to small cerebral arteries, the characteristic recurrent lacunar strokes, while impaired haematopoiesis and immune function account for cytopenias and immunodeficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Primary central nervous system vasculitis and other causes of paediatric stroke
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing for biallelic ADA2 variants
Brain MRI and MR angiography to detect lacunar strokes and vasculopathy
Inflammatory markers and full blood count for cytopenias
Immunoglobulin levels and lymphocyte subsets to assess immunodeficiency
Skin biopsy of vasculitic or livedoid lesions where indicated
Bone marrow examination when marrow failure is suspected
redFlags: Acute focal neurological deficit indicating stroke
Severe cytopenias or bone marrow failure
Serious or recurrent infection reflecting immunodeficiency
Progressive systemic vasculitis with organ involvement
reference.prognosis: Untreated disease carries substantial morbidity from recurrent strokes and vasculitis, but TNF inhibition markedly reduces stroke recurrence and controls inflammation. Prognosis is worse when severe haematological or immune involvement dominates, in which case stem cell transplantation may be curative.
pitfalls: Diagnosing idiopathic polyarteritis nodosa without testing for ADA2 deficiency in a child
Using anticoagulation or antiplatelet agents that increase haemorrhagic stroke risk
Relying on corticosteroids alone rather than starting TNF inhibition for durable control
Missing the haematological and immunodeficiency components of the phenotype
Overlooking a family history of early strokes or unexplained vasculitis
references: Consensus guidance on diagnosis and management of DADA2
